html:
The Valdivia culture flourished on the coast of Ecuador from about 3500 to 1800 BCE. Its people made some of the oldest pottery in the Americas and small stone and clay figures of women.

They lived in villages of oval houses set around a plaza, farmed maize, beans and cotton, and fished and gathered shellfish. Their pottery and the famous Valdivia figurines, many showing women with elaborate hair, are among the first artworks of settled life in South America.

Valdivia shows that farming villages arose on the Pacific coast of Ecuador as early as anywhere in the continent, long before the Inca Empire. Its people traded spondylus shell, prized later across the Andes, and the early use of cacao in the region comes from a similar time. The site was found in the 1950s.
